> 舍利子，色不异空，空不异色；色即是空，空即是色。

不异 is the whole argument, and it is routinely mistranslated in both directions.

"Form is not different from emptiness" is heard as *form is emptiness* — the two words are synonyms, so the second clause is redundant. Or it is heard as *form is basically emptiness wearing a costume* — the visible world is a veil over something else, and the practice is to look behind it.

Both readings fail on the same point: 不异 means not separable, not cut into two independent things. It denies a relation of separation, not a difference of character. Form and emptiness are not one thing called by two names, and not two things joined together.

## The cup, again, and precisely

Bottom of the cup: form. Walls: feeling, perception, formation, consciousness. Conditions gather, and there is a shape. The shape is there, and the hollow inside it is there, and they are not two events. Nobody first builds a bottom out of clay and then, as a second step, produces the hollow; nobody first has a piece of space and then puts a clay bottom into it.

That is why 色即是空 and 空即是色 can be said in both directions without one being the consequence of the other. The way this form exists is already the absence of a form-substance. The emptiness is not somewhere else, waiting; it is this gathering, at the moment of gathering.

## Two escapes, both closed

The book names the two errors the sentence is built to close.

First: treat form as solid. Grasp at appearances, rank them, defend them, and never notice the hollow — this is ordinary life, and it is not stupid, only blind to one half.

Second: treat emptiness as a place to go. Decide the world of form and feeling and thought is the problem, and that the solution is to get out of it into a clean void. This is the spiritual version of the same mistake, and it is harder to see because it feels like progress. It is still a grasp — a grasp on not-grasping.

The sentence closes both in one breath, because it refuses to let either term stand alone. 受想行识，亦复如是: feeling, thought, habit, recognition — same law, no exception. They arise from conditions, they function, they have no fixed nature, and their emptiness is not separable from their functioning.

## Why the metaphor has to be a vessel

The book leans on the 道德经's line — 埏埴以为器，当其无，有器之用 — and then marks the difference.

Laozi's point is utility: the hollow is why the vessel can hold. The emptiness is valuable because of what it makes possible. The sutra's point goes one step further: this clay vessel, the one doing the holding, is itself a gathering with no substance. Laozi says the empty makes the useful. The sutra says the useful is also empty.

Both are true, and they are not the same claim. The first is a lesson in design; the second is a lesson in the absence of a designer.

## The test

Take a cup off your desk. Look at it until you can see the hollow and the wall at the same time — not alternately, not as a before-and-after. Most people can hold one, or the other, or flip between them. Holding both at once for ten seconds is the exercise.

Then try it on a person. That is where 不异 stops being a sentence.
